book.title: Calm Parents, Happy Kids
book.author: Dr. Laura Markham
book.description: Calm Parents, Happy Kids is the UK version of Dr Laura Markham's hugely successful and ground-breaking book, Peaceful Parent, Happy Kids. Now adapted for UK audiences, this practical and inspiring book reveals a three step programme that will transform family life. Most parenting books focus on changing a child's behaviour, but the truth is that children only change when their relationship with their parents changes. In Calm Parents, Happy Kids, Dr Laura Markham introduces an approach to parenting that eliminates threats, power struggles and manipulation, in favour of setting limits with empathy and communication. Bringing together the latest research in brain development with a focus on emotional awareness (for both parents and children), it will appeal to all parents who don’t want to force their children into compliance and lose their temper, but want to keep calm and help their children want to behave.

note.text: Now that I've finished the book, I want to discuss some thoughts about its structure. The book has three parts: Part 1 is Regulating Yourself, Part 2 is Fostering Connection, and Part 3 is Coaching, Not Controlling.

Part 1 makes complete sense. The difficult part of parenting is not the kid — it's yourself. It's difficult not to shout, not to punish, and of course it can be difficult not to hit. So the foundational thing is that you need to regulate yourself, to control your own impulses. Kids will be kids; by definition they don't have a lot of control. You need to be the adult in the room. The first thing you can control is yourself.

Part 2, Fostering Connection, is very important to me. It says very deep things, such as about defiance. Kids can be defiant very early — three, four, five years old. The book says that defiance is not a problem of discipline but a problem of relationship. The answer to defiance is not to punish and discipline the kids; the solution is to build a stronger bond with them. The author sets out connection as the foundational thing between parents and kids and gives a lot of hints and guides on how to do that.

Part 3 is about guiding your kids now that you have regulation and connection. It's the only part with more than one chapter — it has three: (1) Raising a Child Who Can Manage Himself — Emotion Coaching, (2) Raising a Child Who Wants to Be Helped — Dare Not to Discipline, and (3) Raising a Child Who Achieves with Joy and Self-Esteem — Mastery Coaching. These chapters build on top of regulating yourself and fostering connection. Without self-regulation and without the connection, you cannot do any of this coaching.
Overall, the structure of this book is very solid.

note.text: Here's one example of the difference in my behavior with my big kid after reading this book. I usually happen to bicker with my six-year-old. She's a wonderful kid but she can have some attitude, and as my wife describes it, we do some bickering. Yesterday was the first day after a long one-week trip, and I assumed the transition from traveling back to being home could be difficult. In the morning she was cross with me and shouted at me — the way kids shout, like "I don't know how to do this thing!" or "Dad, come and see!" What I used to do before was get so cross that I'd tell her, "You are being very impolite with me, and as a consequence I will not talk to you this whole morning." It sounds childish, but it happened. But yesterday I conveyed the same substance, the same message, but differently. The truth is I was very upset and didn't feel like continuing to talk to her at that moment. But instead of saying "I will not talk to you this morning," what I literally said was: "Our conversation is making me very cross and upset right now, so I don't feel like continuing this because I might say something stupid. I'm going to stop this conversation now and retreat, and when I feel better again, I'll come back and talk to you." I feel better about that because it was truer to my real emotion. It was transparent — my kid could see me regulating my own emotion, so I think I also modeled regulation for her. Then we got back together, joked about it, and moved on without hard feelings. That's just one example of my day-to-day after reading Calm Parents, Happy Kids.

note.text: The theme of this chapter is coaching children on mastery. There is a lot of coherence with what I have read elsewhere about child development, especially with Montessori principles. But the approach in this book is different. The difference is that the main topic is not knowledge of principles and milestones — it's the attitude and state of mind of the parents.

This is important because when I read aspirational books about Montessori, like "Montessori from the Start," I tend to develop a very demanding view of my children. Of course I love them beyond limit, but the book makes me more demanding of them. For example, they say children at 15 months old can fix their own breakfast. It's possible and desirable, but it makes me more demanding. The demanding side can also be harmful — expecting something from a book to happen on the same timeline with my own children.

This book talks about something different: the state of mind of the parents. It insists that the anxiety of the parents is what creates extra challenges for the child. This is coherent with the theme of the book from the beginning — restraint of the parents and fighting anxiety in raising kids.

The irony is that out of our desire to help our children succeed and our own anxieties about whether we and they are good enough, we try to mould them using techniques that backfire and destroy the joy they take in developing their own mastery. We over-stimulate, over-assist, over-protect, over-schedule, and over-control, all of which we'll talk more about in this chapter.

The tools to help with the right state of mind are the same: unconditional love, respect, and scaffolding — as in modeling for them. That's the essence of this final chapter: raising a child who achieves with joy and self-esteem.

note.text: Let's say she wasn't soothed as an infant but often was left to cry. As a result, she's reactive and prone to throw tantrums easily. Unfortunately, her parents, who are well-meaning but ill-informed, tell her that they'll leave her in the shopping center if she doesn't pull herself together. So her abandonment radar is always scanning for danger. Because her working model of relationships is one in which someone withholds what she needs, she's fiercely needy and emotionally demanding. By the time she was a toddler, her challenging personality got her into constant power struggles with her parents. She's concluded that she can't count on her parents to help her with her emotions, so she rigidly tries to keep her feelings at bay. Unfortunately, repression only works temporarily, so she's frequently swamped by her emotions.

I often say that reading a book is like having a conversation with the author and seeing what they try to do, seeing what the challenges are that they're having in transmitting these messages. I can feel this hard, difficult for her, talking about this topic. To be at the same time very factual, very knowledge-driven, but also somewhere high with emotion because you feel the pain when she writes this and thinks about the children and the scenarios that she must have seen and understood. That's a part of the conversation with the author that I usually cherish when reading good books.

note.text: That doesn't mean 6-9 year olds always behave however. They need repeated reminders to do simple things. Some sibling squabbles, famously, come from the weak feelings they are still learning to manage.

I find these words very relevant and highly actionable to me personally. They convey real concepts and real behaviors and can be action-driven. I really like that. I appreciate this book so far.

note.text: After a while of pausing reading books to switch to reading technical papers on AI and LLM, I returned back to reading books. My wife has read this book at least maybe twice, and it's one of her favorite books on parenting — she even bought the second book, Calm Parents, Happy Siblings.

I started reading this book expecting two things. First, to persist on good parenting behaviors that I already know of but fail to practice sometimes. One of the benefits of reading books is that even if you already know something, you have more time to let it simmer and digest and sink in. I look forward to having that effect reading this book.
The second thing I expect from this is that it gives me a more structured way to think about building connection with my kids, about coaching, and about regulating myself.
